hits.text:
OpenAI’s studio integration lands in Blender this month, and the interesting part is that it refuses to generate anything twice

Most tools race to produce assets. This one spends its first pass deciding what already exists and should never be made again.

> INDEX - the studio’s entire asset library read and described, not just filenamed
> MATCH - every new request checked against that index before a single polygon is made
> REUSE - a close enough match returned as a link to the original, not as a copy
> ADAPT - near misses modified from the existing asset instead of built from nothing
> MAKE - only genuinely new requests sent to generation
> FILE - whatever is produced indexed immediately, so the next request can find it

Studios already own most of what they keep rebuilding. They just cannot find it.

A library with ten thousand assets and no semantic index is the same as an empty one. Nobody searches it, so everyone remodels.

Generative tools made that worse. Producing a new chair became faster than locating the three chairs already on disk.

The adapt step is the quiet win. A modified existing asset inherits its materials, its scale and its pipeline history.

Every reuse also keeps the library coherent, instead of filling it with near-duplicates nobody can tell apart.

The index format, the match threshold and a full reuse log are laid out underneath.

hits.text:
This is f*cking insane.

Chinese researchers just dropped "The End of Loop Engineering" four months after the term was invented. Fastest death of a discipline I've seen.

The claim in one sentence: the run is the only thing that knows when it is finished.

Every loop you have ever written had a cap, a budget and an exit condition decided before the first action. The paper calls all three the same mistake.

What replaces them is almost nothing: a verifier the agent cannot fool (tests, compiler, diff) and a memory of its last three states.

> Verifier passes -> done, no extra iteration.
> Three identical states -> hand it to a human with the full trace.
> Anything else -> act again.

Across 2,400 runs that ended at the wrong moment 4% as often as a fixed cap, with 2,391 self-stops and 9 escalations.

So the loop engineer leaves and one script stays: the check that says the work is done. You write that. The agent writes the ending.

Loop engineering turns disposable. The check turns into the job.

That is exactly what I run and documented below: one verifier, 300 Kimi K3 workers, zero caps written by me.

One line to remember: the exit is observed, never authored ↓

THIS IS A PURE F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: you stop writing agent configs by hand. One prompt, and Opus 5.5 writes the entire swarm for you.

By hand that is 16 prompts, 16 tool configs, 16 test harnesses and 2,312 lines you type yourself. Here you type one line.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model opus "build REA swarm ×16 for legacy/"

here's the split:
→ Opus 5.5 reads 578 files and splits them into 16 services
→ it writes 16 specs in parallel, 1,037 lines, no templates
→ every spec becomes one REA agent, one reverse-engineer per service
→ each agent gets tested as it lands, 3/48 checks already green at 3 minutes

the part everyone gets wrong: they hand-write every agent and then wonder why 16 of them drift apart.

here one architect writes all 16 specs from the same read of the codebase, so every agent is wired the same way and nothing gets forgotten.

REA is the piece doing the real work underneath: each agent reverse-engineers its own service, dry-runs on three files first, then writes its spec from what it actually found, not from what you guessed.

you wrote 1 line. Opus wrote 1,037.

Opus architects. REA reverse-engineers. The swarm builds itself.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which service, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the architect only sees the ones that actually split

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 runs as architect, reads the repo and splits it into services
> it writes one spec per service, all 16 in parallel, from a single read
> every spec spawns one REA agent that reverse-engineers that service
> each agent dry-runs on a few files before writing anything
> specs get tested as they land, the architect monitors all 16 in flight
> Opus 5.5 deploys once every spec is ready
JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:

1. Run the main session on Opus 5.5 as an architect that writes agent specs, never agent code by hand.
2. Point it at a repo, let it split the repo into services and write one spec per service, all in parallel from a single read.
3. Every spec spawns one REA agent that reverse-engineers its own service and dry-runs on a few files before writing anything.
4. Test each spec as it lands, never wait for all of them to finish first.
5. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: no agent ships until its spec passes its own checks.
6. Route deterministic forks (service choice, tool choice, retries) through JEV.

Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

↳

save it, it'll come in handy.

Claude Code has a built-in research mode that fact-checks itself before it answers.

/deep-research [your question]

It sends agents to search from several angles, pulls the sources, cross-checks them against each other, votes on every claim and gives you one cited report. Claims that don't survive the cross-check get dropped.

Want that for any task? Start your prompt with "ultracode:" and Claude writes a workflow that runs many agents in parallel instead of working one step at a time.

Prompts that work, from Anthropic's docs:

ultracode: audit every API endpoint under src/routes/ for missing auth checks, and adversarially verify each finding before reporting it

use a workflow to run npx tsc --noEmit and keep fixing the errors until the type check passes or two rounds in a row make no progress

use a workflow to find flaky tests: run the suite repeatedly and stop once two rounds in a row find nothing new

use a workflow to research how our three competitors handle rate limiting, read their docs and changelogs in parallel, then compare the approaches

Type /workflows to watch every agent live, and press s to save a run as your own command.

Works on all paid plans. On Pro, turn on Dynamic workflows in /config first. Workflows use more tokens, so try one folder before the whole repo.

SAVE THIS: Anthropic, OpenAI, Cloudflare and Google have all released AI tools that hunt security bugs in your code. Here's each one and how to run it.

1. Claude Security by Anthropic
A team of agents maps your app, builds a threat model, hunts through every component and checks each finding independently. It can turn confirmed bugs into patch files.
/plugin install claude-security@claude-plugins-official
Then type /claude-security

2. Codex Security by OpenAI (11.1K stars)
Scans a whole repo, one folder or just your latest changes, validates what it finds, writes patches and drafts a SECURITY.md.
npm install --global @openai/codex-security
cs login
cs scan .

3. Security Audit Skill by Cloudflare (31K stars)
Six phases, and every finding is rechecked by a fresh agent that didn't find it. Works in most coding agents.
npx skills add https://t.co/ptOfJggqQB --skill security-audit
Then ask: "security audit this codebase"

4. Mantis by Google (2.5K stars)
Builds a threat model, tries to reproduce each bug, then patches it and attacks the fix to prove it holds. Google says to run it only in an isolated environment.
https://t.co/36azMYVvEz

Run at least one before you ship anything that handles user data.

→ every week, find docs that mention changed APIs and open update PRs

Claude Code has a built-in research mode that fact-checks itself before it answers.

/deep-research [your question]

It sends agents to search from several angles, pulls the sources, cross-checks them against each other, votes on every claim and gives you one cited report. Claims that don't survive the cross-check get dropped.

Want that for any task? Start your prompt with "ultracode:" and Claude writes a workflow that runs many agents in parallel instead of working one step at a time.

Prompts that work, from Anthropic's docs:

ultracode: audit every API endpoint under src/routes/ for missing auth checks, and adversarially verify each finding before reporting it

use a workflow to run npx tsc --noEmit and keep fixing the errors until the type check passes or two rounds in a row make no progress

use a workflow to find flaky tests: run the suite repeatedly and stop once two rounds in a row find nothing new

use a workflow to research how our three competitors handle rate limiting, read their docs and changelogs in parallel, then compare the approaches

Type /workflows to watch every agent live, and press s to save a run as your own command.

Works on all paid plans. On Pro, turn on Dynamic workflows in /config first. Workflows use more tokens, so try one folder before the whole repo.

SAVE THIS: Anthropic, OpenAI, Cloudflare and Google have all released AI tools that hunt security bugs in your code. Here's each one and how to run it.

1. Claude Security by Anthropic
A team of agents maps your app, builds a threat model, hunts through every component and checks each finding independently. It can turn confirmed bugs into patch files.
/plugin install claude-security@claude-plugins-official
Then type /claude-security

2. Codex Security by OpenAI (11.1K stars)
Scans a whole repo, one folder or just your latest changes, validates what it finds, writes patches and drafts a SECURITY.md.
npm install --global @openai/codex-security
cs login
cs scan .

3. Security Audit Skill by Cloudflare (31K stars)
Six phases, and every finding is rechecked by a fresh agent that didn't find it. Works in most coding agents.
npx skills add https://t.co/ptOfJggqQB --skill security-audit
Then ask: "security audit this codebase"

4. Mantis by Google (2.5K stars)
Builds a threat model, tries to reproduce each bug, then patches it and attacks the fix to prove it holds. Google says to run it only in an isolated environment.
https://t.co/36azMYVvEz

Run at least one before you ship anything that handles user data.
